9701-3.6.1.motivate: Why does ice float, even though most solids sink in their own liquid? The answer is in the way water molecules attract one another.
9701-3.6.1.establish: Hydrogen bonding is an intermolecular attraction involving a $\delta^+$ hydrogen bonded to N or O and a lone pair on N or O of another molecule. Water has O–H groups; ammonia has N–H groups, so both form hydrogen bonds. Water forms an extensive network. Extra energy is needed to overcome its hydrogen bonds when it melts or boils, accounting for relatively high melting and boiling points. Hydrogen-bond cohesion gives liquid water relatively high surface tension. In ice, the hydrogen bonds hold molecules in an open arrangement. Melting disrupts some of that arrangement and lets molecules pack closer. Thus ice has lower density than liquid water.
9701-3.6.1.connect: Compare water with hydrogen sulfide: similar small molecules, but water has the O–H groups required for strong hydrogen bonding.
9701-3.6.1.note:
- Hydrogen bonding needs N–H or O–H groups here.
- Water and ammonia are examples.
- Hydrogen bonds explain water’s high melting point, boiling point and surface tension.
- Open hydrogen-bonded ice is less dense than liquid water.
9701-3.6.1.self_explain: Explain why the same hydrogen-bond network can raise boiling point yet make solid ice less dense.

9701-3.6.2.motivate: Why is a molecule with polar bonds sometimes non-polar overall? The directions of the bond dipoles matter.
9701-3.6.2.establish: Electronegativity describes the attraction of an atom for a bonding electron pair. A difference in electronegativity pulls the shared pair towards the more electronegative atom, giving it a partial negative charge and the other atom a partial positive charge. This is bond polarity. A bond dipole has direction as well as size. The dipole moment of a molecule is the combined effect of its bond dipoles, so molecular shape matters. In linear $\ce{CO2}$ the two equal C–O bond dipoles cancel. In bent $\ce{H2O}$ the O–H bond dipoles do not cancel, so water has an overall permanent dipole.
9701-3.6.2.connect: Use the shape learned in molecular geometry before deciding whether a polar molecule has an overall dipole.
9701-3.6.2.note:
- Electronegativity difference makes a bond polar.
- The more electronegative atom is $\delta^-$.
- Molecular shape determines whether bond dipoles cancel.
9701-3.6.2.self_explain: Explain why polar C–O bonds do not make $\ce{CO2}$ a polar molecule.

9701-3.6.3.motivate: How can two non-polar bromine molecules attract one another? Their electron clouds fluctuate.
9701-3.6.3.establish: Van der Waals forces is a generic term for intermolecular forces between molecular entities other than those due to bond formation. All molecules experience instantaneous dipole-induced dipole forces, also called London dispersion forces: a temporary uneven electron distribution creates a dipole, which induces a dipole in a neighbouring molecule. Opposite partial charges attract. Molecules with permanent dipoles additionally experience permanent dipole-permanent dipole attraction between their oppositely charged ends. Hydrogen bonding is a special, relatively strong case of permanent dipole-permanent dipole forces when hydrogen is bonded to a highly electronegative atom; in this chapter the relevant groups are N–H and O–H. Stronger intermolecular attraction generally reduces volatility and raises boiling point.
9701-3.6.3.connect: First use electronegativity and shape to decide polarity, then classify the intermolecular forces.
9701-3.6.3.note:
- Van der Waals forces is a generic term for intermolecular forces.
- All molecules have London dispersion forces.
- Polar molecules also have permanent dipole-permanent dipole forces.
- Hydrogen bonding is a special case of those forces.
9701-3.6.3.self_explain: Describe the sequence that creates a London dispersion attraction between two non-polar molecules.

9701-3.6.4.motivate: Why can iodine melt while its iodine molecules stay intact? Separating molecules and breaking bonds are different changes.
9701-3.6.4.establish: In general, ionic, covalent and metallic bonding are stronger than intermolecular forces. Ionic bonding attracts oppositely charged ions in a giant lattice; metallic bonding holds metal ions and delocalised electrons together; covalent bonds join atoms. Intermolecular forces act between molecules. Melting or boiling a simple molecular substance mainly overcomes forces between its molecules while covalent bonds within those molecules remain intact. By contrast, melting a giant covalent network such as silicon dioxide requires covalent bonds to be broken. This distinction explains why giant structures generally have much higher melting points than simple molecular substances.
9701-3.6.4.connect: When comparing melting points, identify whether the solid is a simple molecular substance or a giant bonded structure.
9701-3.6.4.note:
- Ionic, covalent and metallic bonding are generally stronger than intermolecular forces.
- Molecular melting overcomes forces between molecules.
- Giant covalent melting breaks network bonds.
9701-3.6.4.self_explain: Compare what is overcome when ice melts and when silicon dioxide melts.
